data.title: Disclosure of Sensitive Data in URL Parameters
data.summary: Tokens and identifiers were passed in query strings, where they are recorded in server and proxy logs, browser history, and `Referer` headers sent to third parties. A value that appears in a URL should be treated as disclosed.
data.description:
URLs are logged everywhere by design. They appear in web server access logs, reverse proxy and CDN logs, corporate proxy records, browser history, bookmarks, and in the `Referer` header sent to any third-party resource the page loads.

When the value in the URL is a password reset token, a session identifier, an API key or a shared document link, each of those locations becomes a place the credential can be recovered from — often by people with no access to the application itself, such as whoever reads the proxy logs.

Shared links compound it: users paste URLs into chat and tickets, unaware that the link is the credential.
data.recommendation:
* Send sensitive values in the request body or in headers, not in the query string.
* Where a token must arrive by link, make it single-use and short-lived, and exchange it immediately for a session.
* Set `Referrer-Policy` to limit what is disclosed to third parties.
* Scrub known-sensitive parameters from logs at the point of writing.
data.short_recommendation: Move sensitive values out of URLs into request bodies.
